title: Tracing
html:
This policy owns causal spans, context propagation, sampling, and tracing safety. Observability owns the cross-signal model; redaction owns collection restrictions. A trace explains where execution/time/failure flowed, not every function call or all application data.

Current implementation and accepted direction

ADR-0010 selects OpenTelemetry, W3C Trace Context, and OTLP. The API telemetry bootstrap registers HTTP/Fastify instrumentation before application composition, uses a configurable ratio sampler, and exports through an allowlisting wrapper. Without an OTLP endpoint spans are discarded. The exporter currently normalizes names to http.request and removes events/links; only its declared HTTP/protocol attributes survive export. Do not assume newly added semantic spans, links, or exception events will be retained without changing/testing that boundary.

Prisma instrumentation is registered before application composition, and active trace/span IDs enter structured logs. The exporter normalizes Prisma spans to db.operation and strips SQL, bind values, events, links, and unallowlisted attributes. A Collector is preferred where justified, not mandatory; backend, tail sampling, deployed retention, and client instrumentation are separate decisions. This policy does not require a vendor or deployed collector.

Spans, names, and attributes

A span represents meaningful work with stable name, timing, status, attributes, and causal relationship according to the standard. Typical boundaries are incoming requests, application operations, important database/provider calls, queue publication, and job execution. Root spans begin standalone work with no valid accepted upstream context. Avoid unrelated roots inside one logical operation, spans for trivial helpers, duplicate framework instrumentation, and redundant ORM internals.

Names must be stable and low-cardinality: use an operation or route template, never resource IDs, personal data, raw dynamic URLs, user input, or error messages. Treat names and fields used in queries/dashboards as operational contracts. Prefer standard semantic conventions; add a consistent custom namespace only for actual domain concepts. Safe fields should be typed, bounded, meaningful, and necessary. Justified opaque actor/tenant/job IDs can aid investigation but remain classified and incur storage/search cost.

Never intentionally attach restricted data. Bodies, bind values, rows, credentials, sensitive headers, and arbitrary objects are prohibited by default under redaction policy. Review automatic statement/exception capture; normalize, parameterize, sanitize, or disable unsafe SQL. Prefer safe peer/route and provider operation/result over payloads. Database spans should explain latency, lock waits, and failure without exposing values.

Context propagation and trust

Propagation belongs in transport middleware, HTTP/RPC clients, queue adapters, workers, and integration infrastructure, not manual trace-ID parameters throughout business code. Continue valid supported upstream context only where the trust model permits it; otherwise start a new trace. Parse external headers defensively. Malformed context should not fail an application request unless its protocol specifically requires that behavior.

Trace IDs/context are operational metadata, never proof of identity, authorization, tenant, or privileged routing. Accept only supported protocol fields; untrusted context must not inject arbitrary attributes or sensitive values. Actual principal propagation uses trusted application mechanisms.

Outbound propagation should follow standards and provider support, not automatically send internal context to every third party. Browser cross-origin propagation needs explicit origin/header and privacy review. Trace boundaries and trust boundaries differ: crossing one does not authorize sharing all attributes.

Baggage is not part of the default path. Introduce it only for an explicit distributed-context requirement, with deliberately allowlisted keys; values must be small, bounded, non-sensitive, and necessary across processes. It is not general context storage; do not put email, roles/permissions, tokens, user content, or full tenant metadata there. Most context should remain local. Restore/clear async context after execution; it must never leak across concurrent requests, jobs, threads, or tenants.

Asynchronous causality and trace links

Use parent-child relationships for actual nested work and links where multiple parents, delayed execution, fan-in, fan-out, or independent stages make a tree misleading. Queue telemetry should separate waiting delay from execution time where supported and identify safe message type, consumer, and attempt. Scheduled work without a causal parent starts a new trace.

Immediate retries may remain child spans; delayed attempts may use new linked traces with stable job/event/workflow IDs. Make retry attempts/reasons distinguishable. Duplicate deliveries are independent executions and need not share one trace. Long workflows lasting hours/days should use stages, links, and workflow IDs rather than an unbounded trace. Large batches/fan-out should use counts and selective significant/failed item spans rather than thousands of IDs or descendants.

The current exporter removes links; implementing these semantics requires explicit export-boundary changes and tests, not merely adding link calls.

Outcomes and cross-signal correlation

Span status follows operational semantics. Expected domain rejection or inbound 4xx is not automatically an infrastructure error; an unexpected outbound 401 may be a credential/configuration failure. Record a bounded result/error code when useful. Associate unexpected failures with the responsible operation; do not repeat exception events on every ancestor unless distinct operations failed.

A failed attempt can remain an error child of a successful parent after retry. Preserve meaningful partial failures, timeout distinctions, cancellation, fallback, and circuit-breaker states where applicable. Do not hide degradation simply because eventual completion succeeded.

Logs and error reports should inherit active trace/span correlation centrally where practical. Span events explain one execution; independent searchable semantic events may belong in logs. Do not duplicate both automatically. Metrics answer frequency/distribution questions, not the cause of one trace. Sampled tracing is never the sole required audit/security record.

Sampling and volume

Sampling must preserve useful coverage while bounding CPU, memory, network, storage, and cost. Head sampling is cheaper/early but cannot know the final outcome; tail sampling can prioritize errors/slow traces but needs more infrastructure. Propagate sampling decisions as required by the standard. Keep strategy transparent: an ID in a log may have no exported trace due to sampling, not necessarily broken instrumentation.

Prioritize unexpected errors, important slow executions, and rare high-value operations where supported. Thresholds/rates depend on actual service expectations and traffic; do not invent a universal production percentage. Dynamic/incident changes must be bounded and understandable, not a global unsampling switch for one local issue. Development/tests may sample more while keeping the same redaction rules and isolated exporters.

Bound attributes, lengths, events, links, and spans per trace. Do not emit one event per row/item/loop iteration in large workloads; use safe summaries or justified child spans. Truncation is not privacy protection. Routine health probes, metric scrapes, and low-value static/polling routes should generally be excluded or heavily sampled without hiding critical behavior. Startup/shutdown and migrations normally need logs/metrics first; trace only meaningful diagnostic work. Low-level DNS/filesystem/cache spans need demonstrable value rather than automatic maximum detail.

Export reliability and clients

Exporter/collector outages must normally degrade safely without failing business operations. Use bounded buffering, timeouts, dropping behavior, and safe rate-limited diagnostics for export failures, dropped spans, or saturation. Avoid recursive telemetry storms. Retention and production access apply to traces and third-party processors.

Browser/mobile/desktop tracing is requirement-driven, with privacy and cross-origin safety; mobile also requires battery/network/offline consideration. Local paths, usernames, machine identifiers, and sensitive input are not default trace data. Do not introduce client tracing just to match the server implementation.

Tests and change checklist

Test important propagation across boundaries, malformed external context, async isolation/cleanup, redaction and final exporter output, safe failure behavior, and meaningful causal relationships using in-memory/test exporters. Do not require production infrastructure or assert every automatic span.

Before a manual span/attribute, identify causal value, existing instrumentation, name/standard convention, parent/link relation, permitted fields, trust-boundary propagation, volume, duplicate risk, and tests. For async work, include delay, multiple parents, retries/duplicates, IDs, and context lifetime. Before changing sampling, evaluate traffic, retained error/slow/rare evidence, bias, cost, dropped telemetry, and how results will be reviewed. Preserve current source/export limitations explicitly until implementation satisfies the intended policy.
